panels.rationale: Single axial contrast-enhanced CT (IV and oral) of a real patient, surgery-proven, showing an inflamed Meckel diverticulum with abscess. The contrast-filled tubular diverticulum at the ileal attachment (curved arrow) with a tip fluid collection and fat stranding (arrowhead) is a direct CT manifestation of Meckel diverticulitis, a configured disease. Prior caption triage also keeps it as real-patient radiology of the target disease. [raw subtype: diverticulitis]

panels.rationale: Single axial oral-enhanced CT slice from a real patient (20-year-old woman) captioned as surgically proven needle retention in a giant Meckel's diverticulum. The asterisk marks a fluid-filled, blind-ended tubular structure captioned as the Meckel's diverticulum, and the arrow marks a linear hyperdense retained needle at its collar, both directly visible. The image demonstrates the configured disease (Meckel diverticulum) with an unusual complication (foreign-body retention), fitting the article on complicated Meckel's diverticulum in adults. The captioned blind-ending ileal pouch matches the antimesenteric ileal diverticulum finding; the needle retention and giant diverticulum size are not covered by the vocabulary and are proposed. Presentation is unusual (reported as the first CT documentation of a swallowed needle inside a Meckel's diverticulum), hence atypical.

in_text_mentions: According to the Heinrich classification, modified by Gaspar-Fuentes et al., there are four histological types of EPT: type I—presenting acini, ducts, and islets (complete heterotopia), type II—presenting only ducts (canalicular heterotopia), type III—presenting only acini (exocrine heterotopia), and type IV—presenting only islets (endocrine heterotopia) [19]. 5 out of the 6 cases evaluated belonged to type I and 1 case belonged to type III (Figure 1, Figure 2, Figure 3 and Figure 4).

findings.evidence: Caption: 'Microscopy showing ectopic gastric mucosa [H and E, 100x]'; in-text: 'Sections of the diverticulum revealed heterotopic gastric mucosa, characterized by a mucosal lining of foveolar epithelium and a lamina propria containing both parietal and oxyntic glands (Figures 3, 4).'

panels.rationale: Single-panel H&E histopathology (100x) of resected Meckel's diverticulum showing ectopic gastric mucosa with foveolar epithelium and parietal/oxyntic glands, directly matching the caption and in-text description; this is the classic histologic manifestation of Meckel diverticulum with gastric heterotopia. No age is stated in the caption or in-text mentions (the article title indicates a pediatric case, but per the age rule only caption/in-text evidence is used). No overlay annotations are visible on the image.
panels.attribution_text: Razakh et al. Perforated Meckel's Diverticulum With Dual Gastric and Pancreatic Heterotopia: A Pediatric Case Report.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.103888. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Microscopy showing ectopic gastric mucosa [H and E, 100x]
in_text_mentions: Microscopic examination of the resected Meckel's diverticulum confirmed the presence of dual ectopic tissue and the site of perforation. Sections of the diverticulum revealed heterotopic gastric mucosa, characterized by a mucosal lining of foveolar epithelium and a lamina propria containing both parietal and oxyntic glands (Figures 3, 4). Adjacent to this gastric mucosa, a focal, well-defined peptic ulcer was identified (Figure 5). Furthermore, a distinct focus of ectopic pancreatic tissue was observed, featuring clear pancreatic acini and islets (Figure 6).

in_text_mentions: A 36-year-old male presented with right lower quadrant and periumbilical abdominal pain for 1 month. Ultrasound of abdomen was within normal limits. Contrast enhanced CT abdomen revealed the presence of a MD with thickened, enhancing walls associated with inflammatory changes in the adjacent fat (Figure 4). The normal appendix was identified separately on CT, resulting in a diagnosis of Meckel’s diverticulitis. The patient underwent laparoscopically assisted trans-umbilical Meckel’s diverticulectomy. Histopathology confirmed the imaging diagnosis.

panels.rationale: Single-panel H&E histopathology of a resected Meckel diverticulum from a pediatric case series. The image visibly shows intestinal crypt mucosa (enterocytes) on the left and pancreatic acinar tissue with exocrine ducts on the right, matching the caption and in-text description of ectopic pancreatic tissue within the diverticulum. This is a real patient image of a classic manifestation of the configured disease. [raw subtype: ectopic_pancreas]
panels.attribution_text: Lai et al. Clinical analysis of Meckel diverticulum with ectopic pancreas in children: 3 case reports.. Medicine 2026. doi:10.1097/md.0000000000047794. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: We were able to identify enterocytes and pancreatic cells.
in_text_mentions: Histopathological examination confirmed the diagnosis of MD in all specimens. Ectopic pancreatic tissue was identified within each diverticulum, primarily located at the apex (Fig. 2). In 1 case, the pancreatic tissue extended from the apex towards the base. The mucosa overlying the ectopic tissue showed areas of erosion. Microscopically, pancreatic acinar tissue with surrounding lymphocytic infiltration was observed, and exocrine ducts were identified in 2 cases.

panels.rationale: Coronal contrast-enhanced CT reconstruction from a case report of complicated Meckel's diverticulum; the caption explicitly identifies the blind-ending diverticular structure arising from the antimesenteric border of the distal ileum (red arrow) as consistent with Meckel's diverticulum, matching the classic CT anatomical presentation, and the image is a real patient radiology study of the target disease with visible dilated small bowel loops.
panels.attribution_text: Mora Moreno et al. Recurrent Small Bowel Obstruction in an Adult Male Patient Due to Complicated Meckel's Diverticulum: A Case Report.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.108072. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Coronal contrast-enhanced CT reconstruction of Meckel’s diverticulum. Coronal contrast-enhanced CT image demonstrating a blind-ending diverticular structure arising from the antimesenteric border of the distal ileum (arrow), consistent with Meckel’s diverticulum, with improved visualization of its anatomical orientation.
in_text_mentions: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated dilated small bowel loops with multiple air-fluid levels and a well-defined transition point in the distal ileum. A blind-ending, sac-like structure arising from the antimesenteric border of the ileum was also identified (Figures 1, 2), containing intraluminal material and associated with a prominent feeding vessel (Figure 3). These findings were highly suggestive of Meckel’s diverticulum.

in_text_mentions: d-abdomen associated with vomiting. Abdominal X-ray revealed air-filled distended bowel with multiple air-fluid levels in the central abdomen. Contrast enhanced CT abdomen demonstrated dilated small bowel loops with a transition at the level of the distal ileum. A MD was seen at the level of the transition point, with its tip reaching up to the umbilicus (Figure 6). Diagnostic laparoscopy revealed the presence of adhesions at the site of origin of the MD, leading to distal ileal luminal narrowing. An urgent trans-umbilical laparoscopic removal of the MD and small bowel resection was performed.

panels.attribution_text: Palma Zapata et al. Ileo-Ileal Intussusception Caused by a Meckel's Diverticulum With Ectopic Pancreatic Tissue: A Case Report.. Cureus 2024. doi:10.7759/cureus.51888. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Microscopy image H&E staining of Meckel's diverticulum. A) (10x), B) (40x) It reveals the presence of glandular structures that consist of cuboidal cells, which collectively form the pancreatic acini (PA) exhibiting intense hematoxylin staining. In addition, the image reveals the existence of islets of Langerhans (IL), comprising polygonal cells with voluminous and pale cytoplasm and monomorphic nuclei with classic salt and pepper chromatin. Furthermore, the pancreatic ducts are visible, lined with low cuboidal epithelium that has uniform nuclei alternating with the pancreatic acini. The tissue in question is classified as an ectopic pancreatic tissue type 1 as per the Heinrich classification, owing to the presence of centroacinous cells (CC), excretory ducts (ED), and IL.
in_text_mentions: During the histopathological examination, an MD measuring 3.5 cm x 2 cm with a whitish-yellow invaginated area was observed macroscopically. The hematoxylin and eosin staining analysis of the histological section revealed a Meckel's diverticulum with Heinrich type 1 ectopic pancreatic tissue implantation, and no signs of malignancy were found (Figure 3).

EP are classified using the Heinrich criteria, which distinguish three types. Type 1 is characterized by the presence of acini, excretory ducts, and islets of Langerhans (IL). Type 2 presents acini and excretory ducts, while type 3 only contains excretory ducts. The most prevalent type is type 2, followed by type 1, while type 3 is the least commonly encountered [8]. In our case, the histopathological classification of the PE corresponded to Heinrich type 1, which is less frequent, with only a few reported cases (Figure 3).

panels.rationale: Gross specimen photograph from a real patient showing a resected 5-cm Meckel's diverticulum along an ileal segment, with annotated perforation at the apex (arrow) and narrow base (circle), plus a ruler for scale. The caption, in-text mention, and article title (spontaneous perforation of Meckel's diverticulum in an adult female) directly attribute the specimen to Meckel's diverticulum, so disease attribution is strong. The antimesenteric ileal pouch is visible on the gross specimen and matches the allowed vocabulary; the apical perforation and narrow base are captioned but absent from the vocabulary, so they are recorded as proposed findings. Histology statements (pressure necrosis, no ectopic tissue or malignancy) are explicitly 'data not shown' and not visible in this image, so they are excluded. Spontaneous perforation in an adult is a recognized but less common presentation than classic pediatric bleeding, hence variant typicality. Age group adult is taken from the article title's explicit statement 'adult female'; no ethnicity is stated and no skin is shown.

in_text_mentions: iculum within Meckel's diverticulum. Referencing risk factors for asymptomatic Meckel's diverticulum [4], elective surgical resection was proposed for secondary prevention of complications. The patient consented to laparoscopic Meckel's diverticulum resection. The Meckel's diverticulum resection margins were set approximately 30 mm from the pseudodiverticulum, allowing for complete excision of the Meckel's diverticulum. The resected specimen confirmed the presence of a diverticulum within the Meckel's diverticulum (Figure 2), without evidence of perforation in the Meckel's diverticulum itself.

An inverted Meckel’s diverticulum was strongly suspected because of the atypical structure of the pedunculated polyp. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: H&E histology panel showing heterotopic gastric mucosa within Meckel's diverticulum, explicitly stated in caption and confirmed by in-text pathology description. Gastric heterotopia is the classic and most common finding in Meckel's diverticulum. Human patient specimen from a child. B: H&E histology panel showing heterotopic jejunal mucosa within Meckel's diverticulum, explicitly stated in caption and in-text. Jejunal mucosa heterotopia is a recognized but less common form compared to gastric mucosa. Finding not present in allowed vocabulary, so recorded as proposed finding. Human patient specimen from a child.

in_text_mentions: d hyperechoic (Figure 1). The ultrasound diagnosis was complete MD inversion. After preoperative preparation, the patient underwent transumbilical single-port laparoscopic partial small bowel resection and anastomosis. Intraoperative findings confirmed MD inversion (Figure 2). The patient was discharged 7 days after the operation with stable condition. The pathology of the specimen was consistent with MD. Both heterotopic gastric mucosa and heterotopic jejunal mucosa were present within the diverticulum (Figure 3). A 6-month follow-up revealed no discomfort or abnormalities in bowel movements.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Gross pathology photograph clearly shows a giant Meckel's diverticulum attached to small intestine, with dusky/necrotic appearance; black arrow marks the lesion. B: H&E microscopic panel from the Meckel diverticulum specimen shows transmural necrosis and vascular congestion; no ectopic tissue is present and no configured vocabulary finding directly matches. C: H&E microscopic panel from the Meckel diverticulum specimen shows transmural necrosis and mural congestion; findings are pathological complications of the Meckel diverticulum but are not represented in the configured vocabulary. D: High-power H&E image shows acute inflammatory infiltrate in the serosa of the Meckel's diverticulum, supporting complicated Meckel diverticulum; no configured vocabulary finding directly matches histologic serosal inflammation.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Gross photograph of the resected specimen with a boxed polypoid lesion; attribution to Meckel's diverticulum rests on the article title and caption describing the polypoid lesion specimen. B: Low-power histology of the polypoid lesion showing the transition zone between ectopic gastric mucosa and intestinal mucosa, consistent with Meckel's diverticulum with heterotopic gastric mucosa. C: Higher-power histology with an arrow marking the transition between ectopic gastric mucosa and intestinal mucosa, directly supporting ectopic gastric mucosa in Meckel's diverticulum. D: High-power histology with inset showing ectopic gastric mucosa of the fundic type, confirming heterotopic gastric mucosa in Meckel's diverticulum.

panels.rationale: Single axial contrast CT of the abdomen from a human patient. The caption explicitly identifies a blind-ending structure with calcification and surrounding fat stranding arising from distal small bowel as Meckel's diverticulitis, and the yellow arrow marks exactly that inflamed ileal pouch. This matches the vocabulary finding meckel_diverticulum_diverticulitis_on_ct. Although the article also describes pneumatosis coli/ischemic bowel elsewhere, the figure itself is captioned and visually shows Meckel's diverticulitis, so attribution is to meckel_diverticulum. No age or ethnicity is stated in the caption or in-text mentions.

in_text_mentions: free gas under the right dome of the diaphragm confirming suspicion of a perforation. Fluid-filled prominent loops of small bowel were noted. Pneumatosis coli suggestive of ischemic bowel, extending from the cecum to the proximal ascending colon was seen. A blind ending structure with calcifications was also seen (Figure 1). in_text_mentions: dependent material with mural thickening and surrounding mesenteric stranding [5]. [raw subtype: enterolith] B: Coronal contrast-enhanced CT of the same human patient showing dilated small bowel loops (stars) and the calcified enterolith-bearing Meckel diverticulum with surrounding mesenteric fat stranding, directly supporting Meckel diverticulitis on CT in the context of the article's Meckel's diverticulum enterolith case. [raw subtype: enterolith] C: Caudal axial contrast-enhanced CT of the same human patient showing a small fluid collection with severe mesenteric fat stranding, the inflammatory caudal extent...

panels.figure_caption: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan. Axial (A) and coronal (B) images show multiple dilated small bowel loops (stars). Short segment of terminal ileum showing narrowed lumen and thickened edematous wall (arrow heads). It forms a U-shaped loop around an ill-defined soft tissue enhancing structure (dashed circle) with central dense focal calcification (arrow) and surrounded by extensive fat stranding and traces of free fluid within the mesentery. This structure is inseparable from the distal part of the ileum and is connected to its lumen through air containing pouch (dashed arrow). Caudal axial section (C) shows small fluid collection (curved arrows) with severe mesenteric fat stranding. The expected shape of the obstructed MD is denoted in image A (dashed delay shape). MD, Meckel's diverticulum

panels.rationale: Single axial contrast-enhanced CT slice of a real patient showing a fluid-filled, thick-walled blind-ending tubular structure in the lower abdomen (arrow) in continuity with the small bowel; the in-text explicitly identifies this structure as a Meckel's diverticulum. The thickened wall matches the configured CT finding for an inflamed Meckel diverticulum (synonym: thick-walled ileal pouch). Not a diagram, control, or other-disease panel, and no third-party restriction. Age and ethnicity are not stated in the caption or provided in-text; skin tone is not assessable on CT, so it is null.

panels.figure_caption: An axial CT image reveals a fluid-filled tubular structure in the lower abdomen (arrow).
in_text_mentions: Plain abdominal X-ray revealed air–fluid levels in the small bowel. Contrast-enhanced CT scan showed markedly dilated loops of the middle and distal small bowel with collapsed distal ileum (Figure 1a,b). In the lower quadrant, there was a 4 cm blind-ending tubular structure containing fluid with a thickened wall in continuity with the small bowel. The structure was deemed to be a Meckel’s diverticulum (Figure 2a,b). A band-like lesion was demonstrated with multiplanar reconstructions in the adjacent mesentery (Figure 3).

panels.rationale: Single-panel videocapsule endoscopy figure from a case series of Meckel diverticulum (Case 2). The article title is disease-focused (Meckel diverticulum case series) and the in-text states that capsule endoscopy revealed a luminal duplication in the terminal ileum; the image visually shows an ileal outpouching consistent with an antimesenteric ileal pouch (Meckel diverticulum). Real human-patient endoscopic image with no annotations; the manifestation (ileal pouch/diverticulum) is tagged with the matching vocabulary key, and the endoscopic description of the luminal duplication is added as a proposed finding. Patient is a 16-year-old (adolescent); ethnicity explicitly stated as caucasian in the in-text.

in_text_mentions: A 16-year-old caucasian female had past medical history irrelevant. She was admitted due to melena lasting for 24 h. On admission she initiated hematochezia and pale but normotensive. The hemoglobin was 12.9 g/dl on admission but dropped to 7.1 g/dl 24 h later, requiring blood transfusions. Also the upper endoscopy was normal and on the ileocolonoscpy she had fresh clots in the ileum, without other relevant lesions. Then a VCE (PillCam SB 2®) was used revealing a luminal duplication on the terminal ileum (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Single axial contrast-enhanced CT image from a case report of complicated Meckel's diverticulum in an adult male. The caption and in-text explicitly identify a blind-ending, sac-like structure arising from the antimesenteric border of the terminal ileum containing intraluminal material, consistent with Meckel's diverticulum, and the red arrow annotates the structure. This is a real patient radiology image directly demonstrating the target disease, so it is included with the CT-category Meckel finding from the allowed vocabulary.
panels.attribution_text: Mora Moreno et al. Recurrent Small Bowel Obstruction in an Adult Male Patient Due to Complicated Meckel's Diverticulum: A Case Report.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.108072. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Axial contrast-enhanced CT showing Meckel’s diverticulum. Axial contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) image demonstrating a blind-ending, sac-like structure arising from the antimesenteric border of the terminal ileum (arrow), containing intraluminal material, consistent with Meckel’s diverticulum.
in_text_mentions: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated dilated small bowel loops with multiple air-fluid levels and a well-defined transition point in the distal ileum. A blind-ending, sac-like structure arising from the antimesenteric border of the ileum was also identified (Figures 1, 2), containing intraluminal material and associated with a prominent feeding vessel (Figure 3). These findings were highly suggestive of Meckel’s diverticulum.

The caption directly describes a diverticulum containing a pedunculated polyp (arrow), establishing the antimesenteric ileal pouch of Meckel diverticulum on gross examination. The disease attribution is explicit in both the caption and the article title. B: Companion gross photograph of the same resected specimen with the diverticulum retracted, showing the ulceration adjacent to the polypoid lesion (arrowhead). in_text_mentions: r investigations and operative records, a technetium-99m RBC scintigraphy was performed. The scan demonstrated tracer accumulation in the ascending colon and hepatic flexure; however, the findings remained non-specific and failed to accurately localize the source of bleeding. In view of the persistent clinical suspicion and the equivocal radionuclide findings, a CECT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with CT enterography was subsequently obtained. This revealed a 1.8 cm blind-ending tubular structure arising from the mid-ileum, suggestive of a diverticulum and highly suspicious for MD (Figure 2).

A: Low-power H&E of the resected mesenteric Meckel's diverticulum showing the full wall layers (true diverticulum); in-text cites Figure 4A for lining epithelium with interspersed gastric mucosa, supporting ectopic gastric mucosa in MMD. in_text_mentions: Histopathological examination confirmed the diagnosis of MMD. Microscopic sections from the diverticulum revealed a true diverticulum, which was identified by the presence of all the layers of intestine. The lining epithelium was mostly small intestinal mucosal tissue with interspersed gastric mucosal tissue (Figures 4A, 4B). Special stain using Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) highlighted the neutral mucin in the lining epithelium, confirming its gastric nature (Figure 4C). No evidence of metaplasia, dysplasia, or malignancy was seen.

panels.rationale: Single-panel H&E histopathology of the surgically resected small-intestinal Meckel diverticulum from the neonate in this case report. Caption states 'Histopathological findings confirmed a MD' and the in-text describes the specimen as showing acute inflammatory changes; the slide shows ileal mucosa with dense transmural-type acute inflammatory infiltrate, consistent with MD diverticulitis. Disease attribution is directly supported by the caption; the inflammation finding is supported by both the in-text phrase and the visible histology. No ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue is identifiable from the caption or image, so none is claimed. [raw subtype: diverticulitis]

in_text_mentions: foetus got 5 points when 5 min. Subsequently, the foetus was rescued by keeping warm and positive pressure ventilation by mask resuscitation bag. And then the foetus got 9 points because the reflex irritability was not the best after rescue. The foetus was finally transferred to the neonatology department. During the operation, the surgeon explored the small intestine MD, with a 360° twist and local necrosis without perforation (Figure 3). The MD was removed and sent for pathological examination, which showed acute inflammatory changes (Figure 4). Finally, the mother and the foetus recovered.

panels.rationale: Single intraoperative gross image of a real infant patient showing a Meckel's diverticulum with a blue arrow marking the perforated tip, directly matching the target disease. Caption supports the diagnosis and perforation, while age is stated as infant in the article/in-text.

panels.figure_caption: A Meckel's diverticulum was identified 60 cm proximal to the ileocecal valve, with the tip of the diverticulum showing perforation (blue arrow).
in_text_mentions: xploratory laparotomy. At the beginning of the procedure, a significant amount of turbid pus was observed leaking from the abdominal cavity. An MD was identified 60 cm proximal to the ileocecal valve, with the tip of the diverticulum showing perforation (Figure 2). An enterectomy, including the removal of the MD, was performed, followed by an end-to-end anastomosis. The postoperative period was uneventful; the infant began oral intake on the third postoperative day and was discharged on the eighth postoperative day. The histological report confirmed a perforated MD with ectopic gastric mucosa.

panels.rationale: Single-panel coronal contrast-enhanced abdominal CT from a case report titled 'Spontaneous Perforation of Meckel's Diverticulum in a 37-Year-Old Woman'. The image visibly shows a blind-ending tubular ileal structure with focal wall thickening and discontinuity plus surrounding fat stranding (marked by the red arrow), matching the caption and in-text description of perforated Meckel diverticulum. Real diagnostic patient imaging, no third-party restriction; age 37 gives adult; no ethnicity stated; skin tone not applicable to CT. Perforation is a recognized but less common presentation of Meckel diverticulum, hence variant.
panels.attribution_text: Darayseh et al. Spontaneous Perforation of Meckel's Diverticulum in a 37-Year-Old Woman: A Case Report.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.95304. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Coronal section contrast-enhanced CT showing perforated Meckel’s diverticulum (interrupted wall). The red arrow is pointing to a blind-ending, tubular structure arising from the distal ileum, with focal wall thickening and discontinuity, surrounded by fat stranding and inflammatory changes. This radiologic appearance is consistent with a perforated Meckel’s diverticulum.
in_text_mentions: Upon further review of the CT images, however, additional abnormalities were identified. The coronal section demonstrated a blind-ending tubular structure arising from the distal ileum with focal wall thickening and discontinuity, surrounded by fat stranding and inflammatory changes, consistent with a perforated MD (Figure 1). The axial section further highlighted the diverticulum with adjacent localized air, again suggesting perforation (Figure 2).

in_text_mentions: Macroscopic examination of the intussuscepted portion of the small bowel appeared dusky and hemorrhagic (Figure 4). panels.rationale: Single axial contrast-enhanced abdominal CT with a red circle marking a small blind-ending ileal outpouching. The caption explicitly identifies it as a Meckel's diverticulum arising from the anti-mesenteric aspect of the ileum within a parastomal hernia, and the article title and in-text mention confirm the diagnosis. This is a real human-patient radiology image showing the target disease, so it is included. The antimesenteric ileal pouch finding is directly supported by the caption; the parastomal-hernia location and CT blind-ending pouch are noted as proposed findings because they are not covered by the supplied vocabulary. No inflammation is described, so the diverticulitis-on-CT key is not used.

in_text_mentions: Clinical presentation of this diverticulum, if not asymptomatic, is gastrointestinal bleeding, bowel obstruction or inflammation/perforation [2]. Attempting to diagnose MD using CT imaging in patients with generic symptoms of abdominal pain or bleeding has an impressively low yield – often indistinguishable from adjacent loops of small bowel – thus a majority in adult patients are detected incidentally during surgery [3]. In the present case, after confirming the finding operatively, a close retrospective review of the CT identified the diverticulum (Fig. 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Axial enhanced CT shows a right lower quadrant caliber change (arrow) in a case of axial torsion of Meckel's diverticulum; the target disease is directly supported by the article title and caption confirmation of MD. B: Coronal plain CT shows an abscess-like lesion in the lower abdomen/pelvis (asterisk); the caption states this was retrospectively confirmed as Meckel's diverticulum. C: Coronal enhanced CT shows an abscess-like lesion (asterisk) near the site of the caliber change; the caption identifies it as retrospectively confirmed Meckel's diverticulum.

panels.figure_caption: (A) Enhanced CT on day 8 showing the persistent caliber change in the right lower quadrant (arrow). (B) Plain CT at admission and (C) enhanced CT on day 8 showing an abscess-like appearance (asterisk), which was retrospectively confirmed as MD. CT, computed tomography; MD, Meckel’s diverticulum
in_text_mentions: The severe abdominal pain persisted, and a high fever (38.6℃) developed; therefore, blood tests and enhanced CT were performed on day 8. Laboratory examination showed elevation of the white blood cell count (23,700/µL) and C-reactive protein concentration (19.6 mg/dL). Enhanced CT showed persistent caliber change in the right lower quadrant (Figure 3A). Ascites had also developed, and an abscess-like appearance (retrospectively observed on plain CT at admission as shown in Figure 3B) was observed near the site of the caliber change (Figure 3C).

of the torsion of the MD, whereas WSC enters the MD under normal conditions [2]. To the best of our knowledge, there are no previous fluoroscopic images of axial torsion of the MD, making the image in the present case the first. Additionally, the location of the MD had moved approximately 2 cm toward the cranial side after the contrast examination (Figure 3B, 3C). This CT finding partially corroborates the abovementioned presumed pathophysiology in the present case. The contrast examination might have triggered the MD torsion and small bowel obstruction, although this is difficult to validate.

panels.rationale: Single axial abdominal CT of a human patient (case 1) with an orange/brown annotation outlining the relevant bowel loop; the article title is disease-focused on Meckel's diverticulum and the in-text explicitly states the foreign body is visible in this figure. It is a real patient radiology image, not a diagram, control, or third-party image. The CT-category Meckel finding is used as the best vocabulary fit; the fish-bone foreign body/ileal perforation is not in the vocabulary and is listed as proposed findings. in_text_mentions: child presented to the emergency room with a 24-hour history of diffuse acute abdominal pain, fever, vomiting, and two loose stools. An abdominal ultrasound showed a small pocket of free fluid in the right iliac fossa (Figure 1), and a non-visualized appendix due to bowel gases. Computerized tomography (CT) revealed dilated central and left lateral abdominal small intestinal loops with left-sided single air-fluid level suggesting closed loop obstruction, and no evidence of intestinal ischemia or perforation (Figures 2, 3). The patient was stabilized with fluids and a laparotomy was performed.

The large air-fluid level loop on the CT scan turned out to be the cyst (Figures 2, 3). The diverticulum was necrotic; however, the bowel was viable and healthy and there was no bowel obstruction. The appendix and the rest of the bowel appeared to be normal. The cyst and pedicle were resected along with a 5 cm length of the ileum, adjacent to the cyst's base. Then end-to-end ileo-ileal anastomosis was performed. The histopathological study confirmed the diagnosis of a measured 9.5 x 8 cm Meckel diverticulum with hemorrhagic necrosis. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Genuine multi-slice CT of the patient's small intestine from a case report whose title establishes the lesion as a Meckel's diverticulum misdiagnosed as a GIST. The axial image shows the hyperdense, well-circumscribed ileal lesion (white arrow) corresponding to the captioned manifestation; the disease-focused article title together with the captioned ileal lesion supports attribution to meckel_diverticulum rather than the pre-operative stromal-tumor impression. B: Second axial CT slice of the same genuine patient study, showing the identical hyperdense ileal lesion (white arrow). The disease-focused article title (Meckel's diverticulum misdiagnosed as GIST) together with the captioned manifestation attributes the lesion to meckel_diverticulum; the mass-like enhancing appearance explains the pre-operative GIST misdiagnosis, making this an atypical presentation. C: Coronal CT reconstruction of the same genuine patient study demonstrating...

panels.figure_caption: Multi-slice CT imaging of the small intestine. (A,B) Axial views show a single nodular hyperdense lesion with relatively well-defined borders, indicated by white arrows. (C) The coronal view demonstrates the corresponding hyperdense lesion, indicated by a white arrow.
in_text_mentions: isible within the intestinal lumen extending from the small bowel to the level of both hip joints, attached to the intestinal wall with a broad base and protruding into the lumen, measuring approximately 0.9 cm × 1.8 cm, with a CT value of roughly 36 Hounsfield units (HU). It demonstrated marked and uniform enhancement on contrast-enhanced scanning with relatively straightforward margins, highly suggestive of a stromal tumor (Figure 2). Based on the above findings, laparoscopic segmental resection of the ileal mass was planned to determine the nature of the lesion and achieve precise excision.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: HE photomicrograph shows a sac-like true diverticulum protruding from the small intestine, labeled as Meckel's diverticulum; this is direct histologic evidence of the target disease. b: HE photomicrograph of the mucosa of the Meckel diverticulum shows atypical columnar epithelium growing in a tubular pattern, consistent with the patient's adenocarcinoma arising in a Meckel diverticulum. c: HE photomicrograph from the Meckel diverticulum tissue shows enlarged spaces covered by flattened atypical cells in contact with cancer, interpreted as suggestive of ectopic pancreatic tissue within the diverticulum.
panels.attribution_text: Inokuchi et al. Ectopic pancreatic adenocarcinoma in Meckel's diverticulum: a case report.. Surgical case reports 2024. doi:10.1186/s40792-024-01843-8. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Histological findings with HE staining. a Photomicrograph showing a sac-like structure within the muscularis propria. The structure is a true diverticulum protruding from the small intestine (dashed yellow line). The cancerous area is shown as a Square b, and the cancer and adjacent tissue as Square c. b Photomicrograph showing atypical columnar epithelium that has grown in a tubular manner in the mucous membrane of the diverticulum. c Photomicrograph showing an enlarged space covered by flattened atypical cells in the tissue of Meckel’s diverticulum and in contact with the cancer. This tissue is suggestive of ectopic pancreas. There is no gastric mucosa, intestinal mucosa, acinar cell, or islets of Langerhans. HE, hematoxylin and eosin
in_text_mentions: a tumor protruding to the contralateral side of the mesentery. Microscopic examination revealed that the tumor was in a true diverticulum and was a well- to poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma (Fig. 3a, b). Enlarged spaces covered by flattened atypical cells were observed adjacent to the cancer (Fig. 3c). These findings suggested that the cancer was derived from ectopic mucosa. No gastric mucosa, intestinal mucosa, acinar cells, or islets of Langerhans were detected. Immunohistochemical staining of the tumor was positive for cytokeratin 7 and carbohydrate antigen 19-9, and negative for cytoke

panels.rationale: Axial abdominal CT shows peri-ileal fat stranding (arrow) in a patient with surgically confirmed perforated Meckel's diverticulum. Although the diverticulum itself is not discretely visible, the CT finding is consistent with Meckel diverticulitis/phlegmon and is reported as the relevant radiologic manifestation.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Coronal contrast CT of a human patient from a disease-focused case report of double Meckel diverticulum with mobile cecum. It visibly shows a giant (145-mm) diverticulum beneath the right diaphragm containing intraluminal hematoma, with the ascending colon displaced to the midline and small-bowel loops on the right lateral side — i.e., a hemorrhagic Meckel diverticulum. Real patient diagnostic image of the target disease; included. b: Three-dimensional CT-angiography vascular reconstruction of the same patient showing the persistent feeding artery (white arrows) arising from the superior mesenteric artery and passing behind the ileocecal artery (red arrows) to supply the Meckel diverticulum. It is a real patient image explicitly captioned as the diverticulum's feeding vessel, so it is included as a diagnostic feature of the target disease, although it depicts vascular anatomy rather than the diverticulum itself.
panels.attribution_text: Okumura et al. A case report of double Meckel's diverticulum with a mobile cecum.. BMC surgery 2026. doi:10.1186/s12893-026-03694-6. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Preoperative computed tomography (CT) images. a Coronal CT image showing a 145-mm diverticulum under the right diaphragm with a hematoma inside (white block arrow). The ascending colon (black arrowhead) is located near the midline, with small intestinal loops (inside the white dashed circle) on the right lateral side. b Reconstructed vascular image of the superior mesenteric artery. The artery feeding the diverticulum (white arrows) originates from the superior mesenteric artery and courses behind the ileocecal artery (red arrows)

We started with a 6-cm upper right pararectal incision (minilaparotomy) for exploration, and the intestinal loop, including the ileocecal region, was exteriorized and examined. The red-arrowed deep-pelvic bowel loop with surrounding fluid collection is explicitly stated to later correspond to Meckel’s diverticulum and to disappear after diverticulum resection, providing disease-specific attribution rather than a nonspecific incidental finding. It is kept as a CT inflammatory/peri-diverticular fluid presentation of Meckel diverticulum.

The internal floating structures correspond to the enterolith named in the title (not present in the vocabulary, so proposed). The perilesional inflammatory changes are mapped to the inflammation finding key (the key is CT-labelled, a modality nuance noted here). No age, ethnicity, or skin is assessable; no on-image annotations are present.

panels.rationale: Single axial contrast CT of the abdomen from a case report titled 'A Rare Case of Giant Meckel's Diverticulum in an Adult.' The caption describes a well-defined fluid-attenuation cystic structure in the right upper quadrant with intraluminal gas (red arrow), a dependent fluid-fluid level (blue arrow), and surrounding free fluid — an inflamed blind-ending ileal pouch consistent with Meckel diverticulitis on CT. Disease attribution to meckel_diverticulum is supported by the disease-focused article title together with the specific captioned manifestation; the prior caption triage also kept this radiology image for meckel_diverticulum. Presentation as a giant cystic air-fluid structure in an adult is a recognized less-common form (variant), not the classic pediatric bleeding presentation. Red/blue arrows and numbered markers are present, so annotations_present is true. No ethnicity or skin assessment is applicable.
panels.attribution_text: Nobles et al. A Rare Case of Giant Meckel's Diverticulum in an Adult: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Challenges.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.107543. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: Repeat CT of the abdomen and pelvis in axial view. There is a well-defined, predominantly fluid-attenuation structure in the right upper quadrant, anterior to the liver, containing both hypodense (fluid) and hyperdense (air) components. The portion marked with the red arrow demonstrates a large intraluminal gas collection, suggesting a segment of bowel or gas within a cystic structure. The portion marked with the blue arrow shows dependent fluid, consistent with a fluid-fluid level within the same structure. There is surrounding free fluid within the peritoneal cavity. No obvious evidence of pneumoperitoneum or portal venous gas is identified. The liver, spleen, pancreas, and kidneys appear unremarkable in this section.

panels.rationale: Single coronal contrast-enhanced CT from a real patient in a case focused on Meckel diverticulum (primary disease key meckel_diverticulum; prior triage route keep, not third-party). The arrow indicates the mid-ileal transition point of a small-bowel obstruction caused by a necrotic ileal diverticulum with features mimicking Meckel's diverticulum, and the right-lower-quadrant ileal segment is consistent with the inflamed diverticulum (meckel_diverticulum_diverticulitis_on_ct). The clearly described obstruction findings (dilated loops up to 4 cm, transition point, interloop and pelvic free fluid) are not in the allowed vocabulary and are listed as proposed_findings. Attribution is not higher because the article title emphasizes that the lesion only mimics Meckel's diverticulum, and the CT shows the obstructing complication rather than diverticula-specific signs such as ectopic gastric mucosa uptake. No age or ethnicity is stated, and the panel shows no skin.
panels.attribution_text: Lopez-Alanis et al. Necrotic Ileal Diverticulum With Features Mimicking Meckel's Diverticulum: A Diagnostic Challenge.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.109387. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Contrast-enhanced CT scan demonstrating dilated small bowel loops with a transition point in the mid-ileum (arrow), associated with interloop fluid and pelvic free fluid. No definitive radiologic signs of transmural ischemia were identified.
in_text_mentions: trast-enhanced CT was considered the most appropriate initial diagnostic modality in this clinical scenario. A contrast-enhanced CT scan demonstrated dilated small bowel loops measuring up to 4 cm, with a clear transition point in the mid-ileum (Figure 1). Associated findings included interloop fluid and a small amount of pelvic free fluid. The bowel wall showed preserved enhancement without definitive radiologic signs of transmural ischemia. No significant abdominal lymphadenopathy was identified. The superior mesenteric artery and vein were patent, with no evidence of thrombosis or embolism.

panels.rationale: Single coronal contrast CT of the abdomen/pelvis from a human patient in the case report 'A Rare Case of Giant Meckel's Diverticulum in an Adult'. The caption describes a well-circumscribed rounded fluid-attenuation structure in the right upper quadrant (red-circled) with intraluminal gas, inferior displacement of small bowel loops (mass effect) and surrounding peritoneal fluid suggestive of reactive/inflammatory changes, consistent with a giant inflamed Meckel diverticulum; the in-text mention ties Figure 3 to the RUQ lesion. Real patient diagnostic radiology, no third-party copyright, prior triage route was keep. [raw subtype: giant]

panels.figure_caption: Repeat CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis in coronal view. There is a well-circumscribed, rounded structure in the right upper quadrant (circled in red) with predominantly fluid attenuation. A small amount of intraluminal gas is seen within the superior aspect of the structure, suggesting communication with bowel or entrapped air. The lesion appears to displace adjacent small bowel loops inferiorly, consistent with a localized mass effect. Surrounding peritoneal fluid is noted, suggestive of reactive or inflammatory changes. No evidence of free intraperitoneal air is identified. Liver, spleen, pancreas, and kidneys appear unremarkable in this section.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Axial CT view of the lower abdomen showing a large irregular polycystic mass connected to the small intestine. The article title explicitly identifies the case as 'Torsion of Atypical Meckel's Diverticulum,' and in-text confirmation places the lesion 130 cm from the ileocecal valve with torsion and congestion, consistent with a torsed Meckel's diverticulum. The polycystic appearance and large size (7.5 cm) explain the 'atypical' designation. [raw subtype: atypical] B: Coronal CT view of the lower abdomen showing the same irregular polycystic mass connected to the small intestine. Combined with the axial view, this confirms a large cystic lesion in the lower abdomen. The article title and in-text confirmation of lesion location 130 cm from the ileocecal valve with torsion support attribution to an atypical Meckel's diverticulum. [raw subtype: atypical]

The presentation is explicitly described as an unusual cause of acute abdomen, hence atypical. B: Sagittal contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showing the same gas- and fluid-filled mesenteric collection (arrow) deep to the umbilicus, extending between small bowel loops. in_text_mentions: umbilical tenderness with no abdominal distension, guarding, or tender rebound. Of note, an umbilical piercing was present, placed three weeks prior to presentation, surrounded by minor skin erythema. A full blood count revealed an elevated white cell count of 16.5 x 103/uL with a relative neutrophilia of 78%. Normal liver function tests, electrolytes, and amylase were noted. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis was performed, demonstrating a small (2.5 cm) air and fluid-filled collection deep to the umbilicus and extending between a small bowel loop (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Single axial post-contrast T1-weighted MRI from a disease-focused article on Meckel's diverticulum with enterolith simulating an intraperitoneal hydatid cyst. The caption describes a cystic lesion with peripheral rim enhancement and adjacent mesenteric stranding consistent with an inflammatory etiology, supporting inflamed Meckel's diverticulum (diverticulitis) rather than a simple fixed peritoneal/hydatid cyst; the in-text mention of interval positional change further supports bowel-related pathology. The panel is a real patient radiology image with a specific captioned manifestation attributable to Meckel's diverticulum via the article title. Presentation as a rim-enhancing cystic mimic of hydatid disease is unusual, hence atypical. No age, ethnicity, or skin findings are stated; the finding key is used for the clinical entity of Meckel diverticulitis although the acquisition is MRI rather than CT.

panels.rationale: Single axial contrast-enhanced abdominal CT from a case report whose disease-focused title diagnoses Meckel's diverticulum with enterolith simulating an intraperitoneal hydatid cyst. The caption localizes a well-defined cystic lesion to the left paracolic gutter with internal low-attenuation rounded bodies (enterolith) giving a floating appearance; the in-text notes mild surrounding inflammatory changes, supporting the CT diverticulitis vocabulary entry, while the enterolith/hydatid-mimic morphology is not in the vocabulary and is proposed. Attribution to Meckel's diverticulum rests on the article title plus the captioned manifestation (the hydatid reference is only an initial suspicion, not the identified diagnosis). Presentation is atypical (left-sided intraperitoneal 'wandering' mimic). No age, ethnicity, or skin is stated/visible; no annotations are present.

in_text_mentions: Initial labs showed microcytic hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin: 9 g/dL). Other parameters were within normal limits. An abdominal X‐ray revealed multiple air‐fluid levels and distension of the stomach and small bowel, prompting further evaluation with a computed tomography (CT) scan. The CT imaging indicated an acute mechanical obstruction of the small bowel, characterized by multifocal ileal wall thickening suggestive of inflammatory involvement and dense matter accumulation in the terminal ileum. Additional findings raised the possibility of a complicated diverticulum Figure 1.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 7 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F, G). A: H&E showing well-differentiated carcinoma; article title and in-text confirm adenocarcinoma arising in Meckel's diverticulum, so this is a manifestation of the target disease. B: H&E showing non-tumor ectopic gastric epithelium (red line) adjacent to tumor; ectopic gastric mucosa is the hallmark manifestation of Meckel's diverticulum. C: MUC5AC immunohistochemistry positive in non-tumor cells, confirming gastric phenotype of ectopic mucosa within the Meckel's diverticulum tumor. D: MUC6 immunohistochemistry positive in non-tumor cells, confirming gastric phenotype of ectopic mucosa within the Meckel's diverticulum tumor. E: MUC2 immunohistochemistry negative; the caption states that MUC5AC/MUC6 positivity with MUC2/CDX2 negativity indicates gastric epithelium of the Meckel's diverticulum lesion. F: CDX2 immunohistochemistry negative; supports the gastric (rather than intestinal) phenotype of ectopic mucosa in the Meckel's...

panels.figure_caption: Histopathological findings at the tumor sites. The histological type of the tumor is well-differentiated carcinoma (H&E staining) (a) Non-tumor cells (within the red line) are in contact with the tumor cells (H&E staining) (b) Immunohistochemical staining of MUC5AC (c), MUC6 (d), MUC2 (e), and CDX2 (f) Non-tumor cells (red dotted line) were positive for MUC5AC and MUC6, but negative for MUC2 and CDX2, indicating the presence of gastric epithelium. Tumor cells (blue dotted line) were also positive for MUC5AC and MUC6 and negative for MUC2 and CDX2, indicating gastric phenotype. Immunohistochemical staining of Ki-67, revealing 70% Ki-67-positive tumor cells, suggestive of a highly proliferative cancer type (g).
in_text_mentions: ed an irregular ulcer at the top with a marginal swelling ( Figure 1 ), and its histological examination revealed a well-differentiated adenocarcinoma adjacent to areas of ectopic gastric epithelium ( Figure 2 ). Immunohistochemistry of the tumor cells revealed positivity for MUC5AC and MUC6 and negativity for MUC2 and CDX2 ( Figure 2 ). Esophagogastroduodenoscopy did not reveal any primary gastric cancer. A retrospective review of previous CT images revealed the presence of a Meckel’s diverticulum. The tumor was therefore concluded to have originated from ectopic gastric epithelium within a M

tive ( Figure 3 ), HER2-negative, and mismatch repair (MMR)-proficient. Repeat CT at our institution revealed rapid tumor growth over a short period, with a Ki-67 labeling index of approximately 70% ( Figures 2 , 3 ), indicating high proliferative activity. Given the gastric-type histology and CLDN18.2 positivity, combination chemotherapy with zolbetuximab plus FOLFOX was started.
